claims.text: In the α-particle scattering experiment, a thin gold foil is bathed in a beam of α-particles and a movable detector counts the α-particles arriving at each angle to the incoming beam.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Most α-particles pass straight through the foil with no measurable deflection, which shows that most of the atom is empty space.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: About one α-particle in several thousand is deflected through a large angle, and a very small number bounce back, which shows that the atom holds a nucleus that is tiny compared with the atom, holds most of the mass, and is positively charged.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Only a small fraction of α-particles pass close enough to a nucleus to feel a strong repulsive push, because the nucleus occupies a tiny part of the atom's volume; the rest of the atom is empty, so nearly the whole beam passes through undeviated.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the nuclear model of the atom, a central nucleus contains all of the protons and neutrons and carries all of the atom's positive charge and nearly all of its mass, while electrons orbit the nucleus.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A neutral atom holds the same number of orbital electrons as there are protons in its nucleus, because the proton charge and the electron charge are equal in size and opposite in sign.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The nucleon number A of a nucleus is the total number of protons plus neutrons in it; the proton number Z is the number of protons in it.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The neutron number N of a nucleus is found from N = A − Z: subtract the proton number from the nucleon number.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The proton number Z fixes which element the atom is and equals the number of orbital electrons in a neutral atom, while the nucleon number A fixes how heavy the nucleus is; the two numbers describe different properties and one is not the other.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Isotopes are nuclei of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so they share a proton number and differ in nucleon number.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Because isotopes of an element share the same proton number, a neutral atom of each isotope holds the same number of orbital electrons and the atoms take part in the same chemical reactions.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Uranium-238 (A = 238, Z = 92) holds 238 − 92 = 146 neutrons while uranium-235 (A = 235, Z = 92) holds 235 − 92 = 143 neutrons: the two isotopes differ by three neutrons and have nuclei of slightly different mass.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A nuclide is written ᴬ₍Z₎X: the nucleon number A stands before and above the symbol, the proton number Z before and below it, and X is the chemical symbol of the element.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the notation ᴬ₍Z₎X the lower number is read as the proton number, not the neutron number; the neutron number is A − Z and does not appear in the symbol at all.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a nuclear process, the total nucleon number A is conserved: the sum of the nucleon numbers before equals the sum after.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a nuclear process, the total charge is conserved: the sum of the proton numbers (with the charges of any emitted particles counted) before equals the sum after.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An α-particle is a helium nucleus, so it holds two protons and two neutrons, carries a charge of +2e (about +3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) and has a mass of about 4 u.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A β⁻-particle is an electron, with charge −e and a mass of about 0.00055 u, which is about 1/1840 of the mass of a nucleon; a β⁺-particle is a positron, the antiparticle of the electron, with charge +e and the same mass as an electron.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: γ-radiation is an electromagnetic wave, so it is not a particle: it carries no charge and no rest mass of its own and is written in decay equations as γ, with nucleon number 0 and charge 0.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Nuclear radiation ionises matter it passes through; α-radiation ionises most strongly and γ-radiation least, while γ-radiation penetrates matter furthest and α-radiation is stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An antiparticle has the same mass as the corresponding particle but the opposite charge; the positron is the antiparticle of the electron.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Because a positron has the same mass as an electron and the opposite charge, a positron is written with charge +e and mass about 0.00055 u, and any antiparticle carries the opposite charge to its partner.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A β⁻-decay emits an electron together with an (electron) antineutrino, written ν̄; a β⁺-decay emits a positron together with an (electron) neutrino, written ν.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The neutrino and the antineutrino carry no charge and a very small mass, and they appear in the decay equation with nucleon number 0 and charge 0, so their presence balances the books without changing A or Z of the nuclei.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: α-particles have discrete energies: the α-particles from a given nuclide all emerge with one or a few sharply defined energies, because the decay passes between two well-defined nuclear states.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: β-particles emerge with a continuous range of energies up to a maximum, because the decay energy is shared at random between the emitted β-particle and the (anti)neutrino; when the β-particle takes more, the (anti)neutrino takes less.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An α-decay lowers the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2, written ᴬ₍Z₎X → ᴬ⁻⁴₍Z−2₎Y + ⁴₂α, because the emitted α-particle carries away 4 nucleons and 2 protons.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A β⁻-decay raises the proton number by 1 and leaves the nucleon number unchanged, written ᴬ₍Z₎X → ᴬ₍Z+1₎Y + ⁰₋₁β + ν̄, because a neutron becomes a proton and the emitted electron and antineutrino carry away the balancing charge and energy.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A decay equation is tested by adding the nucleon numbers across the arrow and the charges across the arrow: each total must be the same before and after, and the daughter element's symbol must match the new proton number.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The unified atomic mass unit (u) is defined as one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12, and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A nucleus's mass in u is close to its nucleon number A, not its proton number, because each nucleon has a mass of about 1 u while each proton contributes one unit to both numbers.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: To convert a mass in u to kg, multiply by 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷; to convert kg to u, divide by 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A quark is a fundamental particle: it has no smaller constituents, and the leptons are fundamental the same way.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: There are six flavours (types) of quark: up, down, strange, charm, top and bottom; the up and down quarks make the proton and the neutron.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The up, charm and top quarks each carry a charge of +⅔e; the down, strange and bottom quarks each carry a charge of −⅓e.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Each antiquark carries the opposite charge to its quark: anti-up is −⅔e, anti-down is +⅓e, and likewise for the other flavours.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A proton holds two up quarks and one down quark (uud) and a neutron holds one up quark and two down quarks (udd); neither is fundamental, because each is made of quarks.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The quark charges confirm the compositions: a proton's ⅔e + ⅔e − ⅓e adds to +1e, and a neutron's ⅔e − ⅓e − ⅓e adds to 0, which is the charge each particle is measured with.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A hadron is a particle made of quarks, and every hadron is either a baryon, made of three quarks, or a meson, made of one quark and one antiquark.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The proton and the neutron are baryons, each with three quarks; a meson's quark and antiquark need not share a flavour, and a meson holds two constituents, not three.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In β⁻-decay a down quark becomes an up quark, so a neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud); in β⁺-decay an up quark becomes a down quark, so a proton (uud) becomes a neutron (udd).

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The quark charges check the direction: in β⁻-decay the quark change is −⅓e → +⅔e, a rise of 1e, matched by the emitted β⁻-particle's charge of −1e; in β⁺-decay the change is +⅔e → −⅓e, a fall of 1e, matched by the positron's +1e.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Electrons and neutrinos are fundamental particles called leptons: they are not made of quarks.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The electron, the positron, the neutrino and the antineutrino are all leptons, and the β-particles and (anti)neutrinos a nucleus emits in β-decay are leptons, not hadrons.

verification.method: Authored originally for CIE 9702 AS topic 11 under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).
